newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Suharto vows support for Burma in Asean, better ties.
newsitem.headline: Suharto vows support for Burma in Asean, better ties.

text.p: Indonesian President Suharto told Burma's military government on Saturday he supported Rangoon's rapid entry into ASEAN and vowed to improve economic ties between the two nations.
Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas told reporters Suharto made this promise in discussions with Burma's prime minister, General Than Shwe, and other officials during a three-day visit to Rangoon.
"The talks were mostly centred on how to enhance economic cooperation between the two countries," Alatas told reporters.

But the minister said Suharto and other members of the 11-strong Indonesian delegation also made clear in talks their support for Burma's rapid entry -- along with Cambodia and Laos -- as full members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

"As far as Indonesia is concerned, we hope the three countries can join as soon as possible," Alatas said. He said Burmese leaders reiterated their appreciation of Indonesia and ASEAN's support for its entry as a full member of the group.
He said neither side mentioned any specific dates for full membership to the seven-nation group.
Suharto's visit to Burma is the last leg of a tour of the three countries that hope to join ASEAN later this year.
International pressure has mounted on ASEAN not to admit Burma on the grounds the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) is suppressing democracy and violating human rights.

Democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi, whose National League for Democracy party never took power despite winning a 1990 election, has urged ASEAN nations not to admit Burma as a full member until SLORC improves its human rights record and starts talks with the democracy movement.

ASEAN, which groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam, follows a policy of "constructive engagement" and non-interference in the internal affairs of its neighbouring countries.
"I would like to reaffirm ASEAN's firm stance that we have never and we will not make as a precondition or a criterion for membership, the intenal situation of a country," he said.
Suharto was expected to meet former Burmese strong man General Ne Win later on Saturday. Alatas said the visit was not on the official agenda.
"It's purely personal," he said. "Obviously these two leaders go way back."
Suharto last visited Burma in 1974 when Ne Win was ruling the country with an iron hand.
Ne Win resigned from politics in 1988 but is still seen by analysts and diplomats as a powerful behind-the-scenes force in the current government.
Suharto returns to Indonesia on Sunday.
